title: The 90-Day Rover That Lived for 15 Years
logline: Two rovers built for 90 sols. One explored for over 14 years, the other found hot-spring silica with a broken wheel.
fictionNotice: Speech balloons are fictionalized first-person narration. Caption boxes are documented history.

hotspots.label: Robotic Arm & Spectrometers
hotspots.engineeringFact: The arm carried four tools: a Microscopic Imager, a Mössbauer spectrometer, an Alpha Particle X-ray Spectrometer and the Rock Abrasion Tool.
hotspots.scienceDiscovery: At Meridiani Planum, Opportunity's Mössbauer spectrometer showed that the small "blueberry" spherules are rich in hematite, an iron oxide that typically forms in water.

hotspots.label: Machined Aluminum Wheel
hotspots.attribution: This is Spirit's story. The twin rovers shared one design, so this model stands in for both.
hotspots.engineeringFact: When Spirit's right-front wheel stopped turning in 2006, engineers drove the rover backward, dragging the dead wheel behind it.
hotspots.scienceDiscovery: In 2007 the dragging wheel scraped away the reddish topsoil near "Home Plate" in Gusev Crater and exposed soil about 90% pure silica, evidence of ancient hot springs or steam vents.

hotspots.label: Dust-Covered Solar Arrays
hotspots.engineeringFact: Both rovers ran on solar power. Settling dust cut their energy, but Martian winds sometimes blew the panels clean, restoring power and stretching the mission far past 90 sols.
hotspots.scienceDiscovery: In June 2018 a planet-encircling dust storm blocked so much sunlight that Opportunity could no longer charge its batteries. Its last contact was June 10, 2018.

comicPanels.comicAlt: Stylized illustration: a rover wrapped in a cluster of airbags bounces across red plains in a burst of dust.
comicPanels.nasaImageCaption: Opportunity in "Eagle Crater," approximately 22 meters (72 feet) in diameter. "Opportunity's lander is visible in the center of the image. Track marks reveal the rover's progress." Mosaic from sols 33, 35 and 36.
comicPanels.nasaImageCredit: NASA/JPL (images and captions courtesy NASA/JPL, via NSSDC)
comicPanels.caption: Summer 2003. NASA launches twin rovers toward Mars, Spirit and Opportunity, each built to last just 90 sols.
comicPanels.dialogue: I bounced across the red plains wrapped in giant airbags!
comicPanels.speaker: OPPORTUNITY

comicPanels.comicAlt: Illustration: a rover driving backward, one front wheel dragging a furrow in the soil.
comicPanels.nasaImageCaption: Spirit's wheels partly buried in soft soil at "Troy", sol 1,899 (May 6, 2009). Its right-front wheel had been dead since 2006.
comicPanels.caption: 2006, Gusev Crater. Spirit's right-front wheel stops turning. The team drives her backward, dragging the dead wheel like a plough.
comicPanels.dialogue: Backward it is. I'll pull my broken wheel behind me.
comicPanels.speaker: SPIRIT

comicPanels.comicAlt: Stylized composite of the twin rovers' stories, not a single real scene: a rover's arm scans small grey spherules (Opportunity's hematite "blueberries") beside a bright churned trench (Spirit's silica find).
comicPanels.nasaImageCaption: Taken by the microscopic imager on Opportunity's "arm," this image "reveals shiny, spherical objects embedded within the trench wall at Meridiani Planum, Mars." The area shown is approximately 3 centimeters (1.2 inches) across.
comicPanels.nasaImageCredit: NASA/JPL (images and captions courtesy NASA/JPL, via NSSDC)
comicPanels.caption: 185 kilograms of compromise between weight, power and survival. Inspect the parts that made the story.
comicPanels.dialogue: Look closer. Every scratch on me is a field note.
comicPanels.speaker: OPPORTUNITY

comicPanels.comicAlt: Stylized illustration: Spirit's dragging wheel exposes bright silica-rich soil beside a layered plateau; steam plumes imagine the hot springs that may have existed there long ago.
comicPanels.nasaImageCaption: Bright, silica-rich soil churned up by Spirit's dragging wheel, 2007.
comicPanels.caption: 2007. The dead wheel scrapes up bright soil that is about 90% silica. Hot water once moved through this ground.
comicPanels.dialogue: My broken wheel found what my working ones never could.
comicPanels.speaker: SPIRIT

comicPanels.comicAlt: Stylized illustration: a lone rover under a dark crimson, dust-filled sky with a dim sun.
comicPanels.nasaImageCaption: Opportunity's last 360° panorama, sols 5,084–5,111, finished just before the 2018 dust storm.
comicPanels.caption: June 10, 2018. A global dust storm darkens the sky over Perseverance Valley. Opportunity has driven more than 45 km, and it sends its final signal.
comicPanels.dialogue: Ninety sols was the plan. Fourteen years was the journey.
comicPanels.speaker: OPPORTUNITY

longPanels.comicAlt: Illustration: two slim rockets lift off from neighbouring launch pads at dawn, shown side by side.
longPanels.nasaImageCaption: Spirit's landing site, the Columbia Memorial Station, at Gusev Crater. "A portion of Spirit's solar panels appear in the foreground."
longPanels.nasaImageCredit: NASA/JPL (images and captions courtesy NASA/JPL, via NSSDC)
longPanels.caption: June and July 2003. Two Delta II rockets leave Cape Canaveral carrying twin rovers, Spirit and Opportunity. Each is built to last just 90 sols.
longPanels.dialogue: Two of us, one month apart. See you on Mars.
longPanels.speaker: SPIRIT

longPanels.comicAlt: Illustration: a ball of white airbags slams into red rocky ground in a burst of dust while a parachute and backshell drift away.
longPanels.nasaImageCaption: "Eagle Crater," about 22 meters (72 feet) across, where Opportunity landed. "Opportunity's lander is visible in the center of the image."
longPanels.nasaImageCredit: NASA/JPL (images and captions courtesy NASA/JPL, via NSSDC)
longPanels.caption: January 2004. Wrapped in giant airbags, each lander bounces across the surface before rolling to a stop.
longPanels.dialogue: Bounce, bounce, bounce… and stop. I'm here!
longPanels.speaker: OPPORTUNITY

longPanels.comicAlt: Illustration, split panel: Spirit rolling across rocky Gusev Crater on the left; Opportunity on dark flat bedrock inside a crater on the right.
longPanels.nasaImageCaption: "Image of the rock nicknamed 'Adirondack' and an image of the rover arm moving towards it." Spirit, Gusev Crater.
longPanels.nasaImageCredit: NASA/JPL (images and captions courtesy NASA/JPL, via NSSDC)
longPanels.caption: Spirit explores rocky Gusev Crater. Opportunity rolls to a stop inside little Eagle Crater, on the opposite side of Mars.
longPanels.dialogue: Two rovers, two worlds, one planet.
longPanels.speaker: OPPORTUNITY

longPanels.comicAlt: Illustration: a rover's instrument arm hovers over pale layered bedrock studded with tiny dark-grey spheres.
longPanels.nasaImageCaption: The microscopic imager on Opportunity's arm "reveals shiny, spherical objects embedded within the trench wall at Meridiani Planum." Area about 3 cm across.
longPanels.nasaImageCredit: NASA/JPL (images and captions courtesy NASA/JPL, via NSSDC)
longPanels.caption: 2004, Meridiani Planum. Opportunity finds tiny grey spheres rich in hematite, nicknamed "blueberries." On Earth, hematite like this usually forms in water.
longPanels.dialogue: Blueberries! Millions of them, baked into the rock.
longPanels.speaker: OPPORTUNITY

longPanels.comicAlt: Illustration: Spirit crossing rocky plains with one wheel ploughing a deep furrow beside its other tracks.
longPanels.nasaImageCaption: A trench dug by Spirit on its way toward the "Columbia Hills." Sulfur and magnesium in the soil suggest a magnesium-sulfate salt.
longPanels.nasaImageCredit: NASA/JPL (images and captions courtesy NASA/JPL, via NSSDC)
longPanels.caption: 2006, Gusev Crater. Spirit's right-front wheel stops turning. The team drives her backward, dragging the dead wheel like a plough.
longPanels.dialogue: Backward it is. I'll pull my broken wheel behind me.
longPanels.speaker: SPIRIT

longPanels.comicAlt: Illustration: Spirit beside a low layered plateau, a bright white streak of soil churned up behind its wheel; ghostly steam vents float in the sky.
longPanels.nasaImageCaption: Bright, silica-rich soil churned up by Spirit's dragging wheel, 2007.
longPanels.caption: 2007, Home Plate. The dead wheel scrapes up bright soil that is about 90% silica. Hot water once moved through this ground.
longPanels.dialogue: My broken wheel found what my working ones never could.
longPanels.speaker: SPIRIT

longPanels.comicAlt: Illustration: Spirit with its wheels half-buried in pale soft sand under a dim, cold sky, frost on nearby rocks.
longPanels.nasaImageCaption: Spirit's wheels partly buried in soft soil at "Troy", sol 1,899 (May 6, 2009). Its right-front wheel had been dead since 2006.
longPanels.caption: 2009. Spirit breaks through a crust into soft sand at a spot called "Troy" and cannot drive out. Its last signal reaches Earth on March 22, 2010.
longPanels.dialogue: Winter is coming. I'll keep watch from here.
longPanels.speaker: SPIRIT

longPanels.comicAlt: Illustration: Opportunity on the rim of an enormous crater, its long wheel tracks winding back to the horizon at sunset.
longPanels.nasaImageCaption: Opportunity at the edge of "Endurance" crater. "The gradual, 'blueberry'-strewn slope before the rover contains an exposed dark layer of rock."
longPanels.nasaImageCredit: NASA/JPL (images and captions courtesy NASA/JPL, via NSSDC)
longPanels.caption: March 2015. On the rim of Endeavour Crater, about 22 km wide, Opportunity passes a full marathon distance: 42.2 km.
longPanels.dialogue: Ninety sols? I've run a marathon.
longPanels.speaker: OPPORTUNITY

longPanels.comicAlt: Illustration: Opportunity on a valley slope under a dark crimson, dust-filled sky with a tiny dim sun.
longPanels.nasaImageCaption: Opportunity's last 360° panorama, sols 5,084–5,111, finished just before the 2018 dust storm.
longPanels.caption: June 2018. A planet-wide dust storm darkens the sky over Perseverance Valley. With no sunlight for its solar panels, Opportunity sends its final signal on June 10.
longPanels.dialogue: My battery is low and it's getting dark.
longPanels.speaker: OPPORTUNITY

longPanels.comicAlt: Illustration: a dust-covered Opportunity resting motionless on a valley slope as a hazy dawn breaks.
longPanels.nasaImageCaption: Opportunity's last 360° panorama, sols 5,084–5,111, finished just before the 2018 dust storm.
longPanels.caption: February 13, 2019. After months of calls with no reply, NASA declares the mission complete. Opportunity drove more than 45 km across Mars.
longPanels.dialogue: Ninety sols was the plan. Fourteen years was the journey.
longPanels.speaker: OPPORTUNITY

extraGame.title: Signal Delay
extraGame.tagline: Plan a sol of driving, uplink it across the solar system, and find out what Mars did with it.
briefing: You can't joystick a rover on Mars. A radio signal takes roughly 3 to 22 minutes to cross between Earth and Mars, one way.
So drivers plan a whole day's drive, uplink it, and wait for the rover to report back.
Your job: plan each sol, reach the pale hematite outcrop, and SCAN it before the mission runs out.
extraGame.rulesNote: These numbers are game tuning, not real rover specs.
rules: Queue up to 6 commands per sol. You have 8 sols.
Tilt over 20° triggers a warning; over 30° the rover stops itself (it may roll on about half a metre); over 40° it tips over.
Soft sand: wheels only cover about 40–70% of the commanded distance, it drains extra battery, and the rover digs in deeper the longer it drives there.
Three sols in a row ending in sand with under 20% progress = stuck.
Rocks stop the drive and log a hazard fault. Turning in place can clip a nearby rock.
Battery recharges between sols, a little less each sol as dust settles on the solar panels.
SCAN only works within 3 m of the outcrop.
extraGame.timeNote: Opportunity's top speed was about 5 cm/s. Drives here are time-compressed.

events.slip: Soft sand: the wheels spun and the rover fell short of the plan.
events.rock_stop: Hazard avoidance stopped the drive: a rock was in the way.
events.turn_blocked: A rock blocked the turn. Back up before turning.
events.tilt_stop: Tilt went past 30°, so the rover stopped itself.
events.tilt_warning: The rover leaned past 20° on this drive.
events.edge_stop: The rover reached the edge of the mapped area.
events.scan_range: SCAN failed: the outcrop is more than 3 m away.
events.scan_ok: SCAN complete: hematite confirmed at the outcrop.

outcomes.won: Outcrop reached and scanned. Hematite "blueberries" like these told Opportunity's team that liquid water once soaked Meridiani Planum.
outcomes.sand: Stuck in a sand ripple. Opportunity spent weeks trapped in one nicknamed "Purgatory" in 2005 and escaped. Spirit got stuck in soft soil at "Troy" in 2009 and never got free.
outcomes.battery: The battery ran flat. Without power the rover can't drive, phone home, or keep itself warm.
outcomes.tipover: The rover tipped over on a steep slope. Real drivers plan carefully to keep the rover on gentle ground.
outcomes.sols: Out of sols before reaching the outcrop. Every sol of a real mission is planned with the same patience.

badge.name: Patient Driver
badge.criteria: Reach the outcrop and SCAN it in Signal Delay.

miniGame.title: Spectrometer Scan
miniGame.tagline: Lock the crosshair on hematite "blueberry" spikes in the soil.
instructions: A stylized soil spectrum scrolls past. The ghost trace shows hematite's reference pattern.
Move the crosshair over a spike that matches the reference, then lock it.
Find all three hematite features in 15 seconds. Wrong locks cost points.
miniGame.controls: Mouse or touch: move and tap to lock · Keyboard: ← → move, Space/Enter lock
miniGame.science: Minerals absorb and emit energy at their own characteristic positions, which gives each one a spectral fingerprint. Opportunity's Mössbauer spectrometer and its thermal-infrared Mini-TES both identified hematite at Meridiani, a mineral that usually forms with water. The spectrum in this game is simplified for play.

artifact.name: Hematite "Blueberry"
artifact.description: A BB-sized concretion rich in grey hematite. Thousands littered Opportunity's landing site, small evidence that water once soaked these rocks.
artifact.badgeCriteria: Score 80% or more on the Spectrometer Scan.

epilogue.label: Imagined future
epilogue.alt: Imagined future, not a real event: an astronaut kneels beside a dusty rover at sunset and brushes off its solar panel. No human has been to Mars.
epilogue.caption: No person has ever stood beside Spirit or Opportunity. But the rovers did get their panels cleaned: gusts of Martian wind sometimes blew the dust off, restoring power and helping both missions run far past 90 sols.

title: The Weight Trade
hardwareName: Apollo 11 Lunar Module Eagle · Descent Stage
logline: To bring the Moon home, Eagle had to leave half of itself behind.
fictionNotice: Speech balloons are fictionalized first-person narration. Caption boxes are documented history.

telemetry.actualLifespan: Descent stage still at Tranquility Base

hotspots.label: Gold Kapton Blanket
hotspots.engineeringFact: The descent stage was wrapped in thin, crinkled layers of metal-coated Kapton and Mylar film. The blankets reflected sunlight and slowed heat loss, protecting the propellant tanks through lunar day and shadow.
hotspots.scienceDiscovery: Leaving this heavy stage behind was always the plan. It became the launch platform for the much lighter ascent stage, and it still stands at Tranquility Base.

hotspots.label: Laser Ranging Retroreflector (LRRR)
hotspots.engineeringFact: A panel of 100 fused-silica corner-cube prisms. A corner cube sends light straight back toward wherever it came from.
hotspots.scienceDiscovery: Observatories on Earth still fire lasers at it. Timing the roughly 2.5-second round trip measures the Earth–Moon distance very precisely and shows the Moon slowly drifting away from Earth, about 3.8 cm per year.

hotspots.label: Passive Seismic Experiment Package
hotspots.engineeringFact: A solar-powered seismometer with two panels of solar cells, built to listen for moonquakes and meteorite impacts.
hotspots.scienceDiscovery: It returned data for about three weeks in 1969, the first seismic readings from another world, and led to the longer-lived seismic network of later Apollo missions.

comicPanels.comicAlt: Illustration (stylized): a lunar module stands on grey plains under a black sky, with Earth hanging over the horizon.
comicPanels.nasaImageCaption: The Saturn V carrying Apollo 11 climbs away from Kennedy Space Center, July 16, 1969.
comicPanels.caption: July 16, 1969. A Saturn V lifts Apollo 11 off the pad. Four days later, on July 20, the lunar module Eagle lands at Tranquility Base.
comicPanels.dialogue: Four days to the Moon. About twenty-one hours on it.
comicPanels.speaker: EAGLE

comicPanels.comicAlt: Illustration: the ascent stage blasts off, leaving the gold-foiled descent stage behind on the surface.
comicPanels.nasaImageCaption: Eagle in lunar orbit after separating from the command module Columbia, July 20, 1969. Its gold-foiled descent stage would never leave the Moon.
comicPanels.caption: Every kilogram lifted off the Moon needs fuel, and that fuel must be lifted too. That is the rocket equation. To carry rocks home, the crew left things behind: boots, backpacks, cameras and the whole descent stage.
comicPanels.dialogue: So I give up my lower half. Take the rocks home.
comicPanels.speaker: EAGLE

comicPanels.comicAlt: Illustration: a laser retroreflector panel and a seismometer with solar wings stand on the regolith, the lunar module behind them.
comicPanels.nasaImageCaption: Buzz Aldrin beside the newly deployed seismometer (foreground) and laser retroreflector (beyond), with Eagle at far right. AS11-40-5948.
comicPanels.caption: What stayed behind was not junk. It was the first science station on another world.
comicPanels.dialogue: They left me with two instruments. One of them still listens for Earth.
comicPanels.speaker: EAGLE

comicPanels.comicAlt: Illustration: gloved hands hold an open metal sample box filled with grey rocks.
comicPanels.nasaImageCaption: The first Apollo 11 sample return container is unloaded at the Lunar Receiving Laboratory, July 25, 1969.
comicPanels.caption: July 24, 1969. Columbia splashes down in the Pacific carrying 21.55 kg of lunar rock and soil, the first samples brought back from another world.
comicPanels.dialogue: Twenty-one kilograms of Moon. Worth every gram I left.
comicPanels.speaker: EAGLE

comicPanels.comicAlt: Illustration: an observatory on Earth fires a thin green laser beam toward the Moon.
comicPanels.nasaImageCaption: The plaque on Eagle's descent-stage ladder: "We came in peace for all mankind." AS11-40-5899.
comicPanels.caption: The descent stage still stands at Tranquility Base, its plaque facing the empty plain. Laser pulses from Earth still find the mirrors placed beside it.
comicPanels.dialogue: Fire your laser. I will send the light back.
comicPanels.speaker: EAGLE

longPanels.comicAlt: Illustration: a giant Saturn V rocket climbs past its launch tower on a column of fire while crowds watch in silhouette.
longPanels.nasaImageCaption: The Saturn V carrying Apollo 11 climbs away from Kennedy Space Center, July 16, 1969.
longPanels.caption: July 16, 1969. A Saturn V rocket, 110 metres tall, lifts Apollo 11 off the pad at Kennedy Space Center with three astronauts aboard.
longPanels.dialogue: Folded up inside a rocket, heading for the Moon.
longPanels.speaker: EAGLE

longPanels.comicAlt: Illustration: the gold-and-silver lunar module drifts away from the command module above the grey curve of the Moon, Earth in the distance.
longPanels.nasaImageCaption: Eagle in lunar orbit after separating from the command module Columbia, July 20, 1969. Its gold-foiled descent stage would never leave the Moon.
longPanels.caption: July 20, 1969. In orbit around the Moon, the lunar module Eagle separates from the command module Columbia. Michael Collins stays aboard Columbia.
longPanels.dialogue: Goodbye, Columbia. Keep the lights on for us.
longPanels.speaker: EAGLE

longPanels.comicAlt: Illustration: the lunar module drops toward a rocky grey plain, its engine glowing and dust blowing outward beneath it.
longPanels.nasaImageCaption: Eagle in lunar orbit after separating from the command module Columbia, July 20, 1969. Its gold-foiled descent stage would never leave the Moon.
longPanels.caption: The computer is steering toward a field of boulders. Neil Armstrong takes manual control and flies past it, landing with very little fuel to spare.
longPanels.dialogue: Boulders below! Easy… easy… fuel's getting low.
longPanels.speaker: EAGLE

longPanels.comicAlt: Illustration: the lunar module stands on a flat grey plain under a black sky, with a blue crescent Earth overhead.
longPanels.nasaImageCaption: The plaque on Eagle's descent-stage ladder: "We came in peace for all mankind." AS11-40-5899.
longPanels.caption: July 20, 1969. "Houston, Tranquility Base here. The Eagle has landed."
longPanels.dialogue: Engine off. Dust settling. We're here.
longPanels.speaker: EAGLE

longPanels.comicAlt: Illustration: a close-up of a ridged astronaut bootprint pressed into fine grey lunar dust.
longPanels.nasaImageCaption: Buzz Aldrin beside the newly deployed seismometer (foreground) and laser retroreflector (beyond), with Eagle at far right. AS11-40-5948.
longPanels.caption: Neil Armstrong steps onto the Moon, followed by Buzz Aldrin. There is no wind or rain on the Moon to blow their footprints away.
longPanels.dialogue: Their first steps. Up here, nothing blows footprints away.
longPanels.speaker: EAGLE

longPanels.comicAlt: Illustration: an astronaut with a gold visor sets down a square panel of prisms, with a winged seismometer and the lunar module behind.
longPanels.nasaImageCaption: Buzz Aldrin beside the newly deployed seismometer (foreground) and laser retroreflector (beyond), with Eagle at far right. AS11-40-5948.
longPanels.caption: Aldrin sets up a seismometer to feel moonquakes, and a laser retroreflector: a panel of 100 prisms that bounces light straight back to where it came from.
longPanels.dialogue: A mirror and a listener. Gifts to leave behind.
longPanels.speaker: EAGLE

longPanels.comicAlt: Illustration: a gloved hand tips a scoop of grey rocks into an open aluminum sample box, the gold lander behind.
longPanels.nasaImageCaption: The first Apollo 11 sample return container is unloaded at the Lunar Receiving Laboratory, July 25, 1969.
longPanels.caption: The crew collects 21.55 kg of lunar rock and soil and seals it in boxes for the trip home.
longPanels.dialogue: Every rock they pack is a reason to leave something behind.
longPanels.speaker: EAGLE

longPanels.comicAlt: Illustration: the silver upper stage of the lunar module blasts off on a bright flame, leaving the gold lower stage behind in a spray of dust and foil.
longPanels.nasaImageCaption: Eagle in lunar orbit after separating from the command module Columbia, July 20, 1969. Its gold-foiled descent stage would never leave the Moon.
longPanels.caption: July 21, 1969. Eagle's upper stage lifts off, using the gold descent stage as its launch pad. Every kilogram left behind is fuel saved for the trip home.
longPanels.dialogue: Go. I'll stay. I make a good launch pad.
longPanels.speaker: EAGLE

longPanels.comicAlt: Illustration: a cone-shaped capsule floats in ocean waves beside three orange-and-white parachutes, with a helicopter and an aircraft carrier beyond.
longPanels.nasaImageCaption: The first Apollo 11 sample return container is unloaded at the Lunar Receiving Laboratory, July 25, 1969.
longPanels.caption: July 24, 1969. Columbia splashes down in the Pacific Ocean, and the recovery ship USS Hornet picks up the crew and their Moon rocks.
longPanels.dialogue: Splashdown! Twenty-one kilograms of Moon, safely home.
longPanels.speaker: COLUMBIA

longPanels.comicAlt: Illustration: the abandoned gold descent stage stands on the silent Moon while a thin green laser from a tiny Earth strikes a prism panel nearby.
longPanels.nasaImageCaption: The plaque on Eagle's descent-stage ladder: "We came in peace for all mankind." AS11-40-5899.
longPanels.caption: Today. The descent stage still stands at Tranquility Base. Observatories on Earth still fire lasers at the retroreflector to measure the Moon's distance to within millimetres.
longPanels.dialogue: Still here. Still sending your light back.
longPanels.speaker: EAGLE

miniGame.title: Laser Bounce
miniGame.tagline: Aim a laser at Tranquility Base and time the light's return.
instructions: The Moon drifts across your telescope's field of view. The retroreflector is a tiny target.
Adjust the aim angle until the reticle sits on the LRRR, then fire.
Light needs about 2.5 seconds to reach the Moon and return. Get one clean return within 15 seconds.
miniGame.controls: Slider or ← → to aim · Space/Enter or the Fire button to send a pulse
miniGame.science: Light travels at about 299,792 km per second. The Moon is roughly 384,400 km away on average, so a pulse makes the round trip in about 2.5 seconds. Halve the round-trip time and multiply by the speed of light, and you have the distance. Lunar laser ranging has used Apollo 11's reflector since 1969.

artifact.name: Corner-Cube Prism
artifact.description: One of the 100 prisms in Apollo 11's retroreflector. More than fifty years later, it still returns laser light to observatories on Earth.
artifact.badgeCriteria: Score 80% or more on the Laser Bounce.

sources.label: NASA NSSDCA: Apollo 11 Lunar Module / EASEP

title: Flight 72
logline: Built to try five flights. It flew seventy-two, then stayed on as a stationary data logger.
fictionNotice: Speech balloons are fictionalized first-person narration. Caption boxes are documented history.

hotspots.label: Damaged Carbon-Fiber Blades
hotspots.engineeringFact: Two stacked rotors, each 1.2 m tip to tip, spin in opposite directions. They have to spin far faster than a helicopter's rotors on Earth to grip air only about 1% as dense.
hotspots.scienceDiscovery: Images taken after Flight 72 on January 18, 2024 showed a damaged rotor blade. Ingenuity could no longer fly, and NASA ended its flight mission on January 25, 2024.

hotspots.label: Snapdragon Processor & Solar Panel
hotspots.engineeringFact: A Qualcomm Snapdragon 801, from the same chip family once used in smartphones, ran the flight software. The solar panel on top recharged six lithium-ion battery cells.
hotspots.scienceDiscovery: Grounded but still powered by its solar panel, Ingenuity stayed on as a stationary testbed, logging weather and avionics data from Jezero Crater.

hotspots.label: Navigation Camera
hotspots.engineeringFact: A downward-facing black-and-white camera tracked surface features many times per second, so the helicopter could estimate its own motion.
hotspots.scienceDiscovery: NASA's investigation found that on Flight 72 the navigation system struggled over smooth, featureless sand ripples, which likely led to the hard landing.

comicPanels.comicAlt: Illustration: a small helicopter sits on tan Martian ground with a large rover in the background.
comicPanels.nasaImageCaption: Ingenuity still attached to the belly of the Perseverance rover, seen by the WATSON camera, March 2021.
comicPanels.caption: February 18, 2021. Tucked under Perseverance's belly, a 1.8 kg helicopter arrives at Jezero Crater. In early April the rover sets it down on the surface.
comicPanels.dialogue: Nobody had ever flown on another planet. I was built to try five times.
comicPanels.speaker: INGENUITY

comicPanels.comicAlt: Illustration: the helicopter hovers above the ground, rotors blurred, its shadow on the sand below.
comicPanels.nasaImageCaption: Perseverance's Navcam watches Ingenuity hover on April 19, 2021, the first powered, controlled flight on another planet.
comicPanels.caption: Mars's air is about 1% as dense as Earth's. To lift off, Ingenuity's rotors had to spin at about 2,537 RPM.
comicPanels.dialogue: Thin air. Freezing nights. One chance at a first flight.
comicPanels.speaker: INGENUITY

comicPanels.comicAlt: Illustration: a close-up of the helicopter, showing its body, legs, solar panel and stacked rotors.
comicPanels.nasaImageCaption: Perseverance takes a selfie with Ingenuity, about 3.9 m away, April 2021.
comicPanels.caption: 1.8 kilograms, two rotors, one smartphone-class processor. Inspect what let it fly.
comicPanels.speaker: INGENUITY

comicPanels.comicAlt: Illustration: the helicopter flies over dunes and a crater rim in low sunlight.
comicPanels.nasaImageCaption: "Castell Henllys" in Jezero Crater, photographed by Ingenuity during its 48th flight, March 21, 2023.
comicPanels.caption: Five planned flights became seventy-two. Ingenuity went from technology demo to aerial scout, photographing terrain ahead of Perseverance.
comicPanels.dialogue: Five was the test. Seventy-two was the proof.
comicPanels.speaker: INGENUITY

comicPanels.comicAlt: Illustration: the grounded helicopter on rippled sand, one rotor blade tip visibly broken.
comicPanels.nasaImageCaption: After Flight 72, Ingenuity photographs the shadow of its own damaged rotor blade, January 2024.
comicPanels.caption: January 18, 2024. Flight 72 ends with a damaged blade. Grounded but still powered, Ingenuity stays on as a stationary data logger on Mars.
comicPanels.dialogue: I can't fly anymore. I can still listen to the weather.
comicPanels.speaker: INGENUITY

longPanels.comicAlt: Illustration: a rocket-powered sky crane lowers the Perseverance rover on cables through a cloud of dust, a tiny folded helicopter under its belly.
longPanels.nasaImageCaption: Ingenuity still attached to the belly of the Perseverance rover, seen by the WATSON camera, March 2021.
longPanels.caption: February 18, 2021. A sky crane lowers the Perseverance rover into Jezero Crater. Folded under its belly rides Ingenuity, a 1.8 kg helicopter.
longPanels.dialogue: Hold on tight. Next stop: Jezero Crater.
longPanels.speaker: INGENUITY

longPanels.comicAlt: Illustration: the small helicopter stands alone on the crater floor while the rover drives away in the distance.
longPanels.nasaImageCaption: Perseverance takes a selfie with Ingenuity, about 3.9 m away, April 2021.
longPanels.caption: April 3, 2021. Perseverance sets Ingenuity down on the crater floor and drives away. For the first time, the helicopter is on its own.
longPanels.dialogue: Okay. Just me now.
longPanels.speaker: INGENUITY

longPanels.comicAlt: Illustration: the helicopter alone under a starry Martian night sky, frost on its legs and a faint glow from its electronics.
longPanels.nasaImageCaption: Perseverance takes a selfie with Ingenuity, about 3.9 m away, April 2021.
longPanels.caption: Its first night alone. Temperatures can drop to about −90 °C, so Ingenuity must keep its electronics warm with battery power until the Sun returns.
longPanels.dialogue: So cold… keep the heaters on. Wait for the Sun.
longPanels.speaker: INGENUITY

longPanels.comicAlt: Illustration: the helicopter hovers a few metres above the ground, rotors blurred, as the rover watches from a distance.
longPanels.nasaImageCaption: Perseverance's Navcam watches Ingenuity hover on April 19, 2021, the first powered, controlled flight on another planet.
longPanels.caption: April 19, 2021. Ingenuity rises 3 metres and hovers for about 30 seconds: the first powered, controlled flight on another planet.
longPanels.dialogue: I'm flying. On Mars!
longPanels.speaker: INGENUITY

longPanels.comicAlt: Illustration: the helicopter flies low over rugged ridges and dark rocky ground, the rover a tiny dot far behind.
longPanels.nasaImageCaption: "Castell Henllys" in Jezero Crater, photographed by Ingenuity during its 48th flight, March 21, 2023.
longPanels.caption: Ingenuity was planned for just five test flights. After passing them, it becomes a scout, flying ahead to photograph the rover's route.
longPanels.dialogue: I'll check the path ahead. Follow me!
longPanels.speaker: INGENUITY

longPanels.comicAlt: Illustration: the helicopter rests under a hazy, dusty sky, a thin layer of dust on its solar panel.
longPanels.nasaImageCaption: "Castell Henllys" in Jezero Crater, photographed by Ingenuity during its 48th flight, March 21, 2023.
longPanels.caption: Martian winter brings dust, weaker sunlight and colder nights. With less power to recharge its batteries, every flight gets harder.
longPanels.dialogue: Dust on my solar panel. Just a little more sunlight, please.
longPanels.speaker: INGENUITY

longPanels.comicAlt: Illustration: the helicopter speeds high above rippled sand dunes at golden hour, its shadow racing below.
longPanels.nasaImageCaption: "Castell Henllys" in Jezero Crater, photographed by Ingenuity during its 48th flight, March 21, 2023.
longPanels.caption: Over nearly three years, Ingenuity flies 72 times, covering about 17 km and climbing as high as 24 metres.
longPanels.dialogue: Planned for five flights. Look at me now!
longPanels.speaker: INGENUITY

longPanels.comicAlt: Illustration: the helicopter comes down hard on smooth sand ripples in a burst of dust as the tip of one rotor blade snaps off.
longPanels.nasaImageCaption: After Flight 72, Ingenuity photographs the shadow of its own damaged rotor blade, January 2024.
longPanels.caption: January 18, 2024. Over smooth, featureless sand ripples, its navigation camera can't track the ground. Ingenuity lands hard, and its rotor blades break.
longPanels.dialogue: Can't see the ground… brace!
longPanels.speaker: INGENUITY

longPanels.comicAlt: Illustration: seen from far away, the small helicopter stands alone on the crest of a sand dune in a vast, empty landscape.
longPanels.nasaImageCaption: After Flight 72, Ingenuity photographs the shadow of its own damaged rotor blade, January 2024.
longPanels.caption: January 25, 2024. NASA announces that Ingenuity's flying days are over. Weeks later, Perseverance photographs its old friend from far away before driving on.
longPanels.dialogue: Go on, Perseverance. I'll stay here.
longPanels.speaker: INGENUITY

longPanels.comicAlt: Illustration: the grounded helicopter with a broken rotor blade stands on a sand ripple at sunset, its small lights still glowing.
longPanels.nasaImageCaption: After Flight 72, Ingenuity photographs the shadow of its own damaged rotor blade, January 2024.
longPanels.caption: Today. Ingenuity can no longer fly, but it stays on as a stationary station, still collecting data on the surface of Mars.
longPanels.dialogue: I can't fly anymore. But I'm still listening.
longPanels.speaker: INGENUITY

miniGame.title: RPM Throttle
miniGame.tagline: Spin the rotors to 2,537 RPM without draining the battery.
instructions: Hold the throttle to spin up. The rotors have inertia, so they lag behind your input.
Keep the rotors inside the lift band around 2,537 RPM for 3 seconds to lift off.
Power use climbs steeply with RPM. Overspeed drains the battery fast, so feather the throttle.
miniGame.controls: Hold the Throttle button, Space or ↑ to power up · release or ↓ to ease off
miniGame.science: Lift depends on air density and blade speed. Mars's air is about 1% as dense as Earth's, so Ingenuity's blades had to spin very fast to lift 1.8 kg. The power a rotor needs rises steeply with speed, so every extra RPM costs battery. The power curve in this game is simplified.

artifact.name: Rotor Blade Fragment
artifact.description: A blade built to grip air about 1% as dense as Earth's. Flight 72 broke it, but by then it had carried a helicopter 72 times on another planet.
artifact.badgeCriteria: Score 80% or more on the RPM Throttle.
